payload.input:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Dragon

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In Christian teaching the dragon is overwhelmingly understood as a symbol of Satan (the devil), the primordial adversary of God and persecutor of God's people. The Book of Revelation makes this identification explicit, calling the great red dragon 'that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan,' thereby also linking the dragon to the serpent of Eden. By extension the dragon symbolizes cosmic evil and the chaotic, God-opposing power that stands behind hostile earthly kingdoms.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Revelation 12:3-9 (the great red dragon who wars against the woman and her child; explicitly identified as 'that ancient serpent... the devil and Satan')",
    "Revelation 12:17 (the dragon makes war on those who keep God's commandments)",
    "Revelation 13:2-4 (the dragon gives his power and throne to the beast)",
    "Revelation 16:13 (unclean spirits from the mouth of the dragon)",
    "Revelation 20:2 (the dragon, that ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, bound for a thousand years)",
    "Genesis 3:1-15 (the serpent of Eden, linked to the dragon via Revelation 12:9 and 20:2)",
    "Isaiah 27:1 (the LORD will punish Leviathan the serpent and slay the dragon in the sea)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Hostile earthly empires and rulers personified: in the Old Testament prophets the dragon/sea monster imagery is applied to Pharaoh and Egypt (Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2), to Babylon (Jeremiah 51:34), and via Rahab to oppressive powers generally (Isaiah 51:9; Psalm 87:4). Many interpreters, especially preterist and historical-critical readers, see Revelation's dragon as evoking or standing behind Rome and imperial persecution.",
      "basis": [
        "Ezekiel 29:3",
        "Ezekiel 32:2",
        "Jeremiah 51:34",
        "Isaiah 51:9-10",
        "Psalm 87:4",
        "Revelation 13:1-4 (dragon empowering the imperial beast)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Ancient Near Eastern chaos monster / combat-myth motif: in academic biblical studies the dragon (Leviathan, Rahab, tannin) represents primeval chaos subdued by God at creation, drawing on Canaanite and Mesopotamian mythology (e.g., Baal vs. Yamm/Lotan, Marduk vs. Tiamat). Revelation's dragon is read as the Christianized climax of this Chaoskampf tradition rather than a literal personal being.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 74:13-14",
        "Psalm 89:9-10",
        "Job 26:12-13",
        "Job 41 (Leviathan)",
        "Isaiah 27:1",
        "Isaiah 51:9"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "The dragon as a symbol of pagan religion, idolatry, or the collective spiritual forces of evil systems (rather than a single personal Satan) — found in some liberal, symbolic, and idealist interpretive traditions that treat Revelation's figures as archetypes of evil in every age.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 12-13 read idealistically/symbolically",
        "Ephesians 6:12 (spiritual forces of evil, used as a supporting frame)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "In some Old Testament passages 'dragon' (tannin) is treated as simply a large creature — sea monster, serpent, or in older KJV usage 'dragons' for jackals/desolate-place creatures — carrying no symbolic weight; a translational rather than symbolic issue.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 1:21 (great sea creatures/tanninim)",
        "Exodus 7:9-12 (staff becomes a serpent/tannin)",
        "Isaiah 34:13 and Jeremiah 9:11 (KJV 'dragons' = jackals)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "This is one of the most settled symbols in biblical interpretation because the text itself supplies the identification: Revelation 12:9 and 20:2 explicitly name the dragon as the devil and Satan. Virtually all Christian traditions—patristic, medieval, Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, evangelical, and most critical scholars describing the author's intent—agree on the Satan identification within Revelation. The genuine interpretive divergence concerns (a) the Old Testament dragon/Leviathan/Rahab passages, where the referent is often a nation (Egypt, Babylon) or a mythic chaos motif rather than Satan directly, and (b) whether the dragon represents a personal devil or a symbolic personification of evil/chaos/imperial power. These are layered rather than competing readings: most commentators hold that the OT chaos-monster and empire imagery is deliberately taken up by Revelation and focused on Satan."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "Satan—the devil as the chief personal power of evil, enemy of God, accuser and persecutor of God’s people.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Revelation 12:3–9 explicitly identifies the great dragon as “that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan.”",
    "Revelation 12:13–17 depicts the dragon persecuting the woman and her offspring.",
    "Revelation 13:1–4 presents the dragon as empowering the beast and receiving worship through it.",
    "Revelation 20:2 identifies the dragon again as “the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan”; Revelation 20:7–10 describes his final defeat.",
    "The identification with the “ancient serpent” connects the imagery retrospectively with the tempter in Genesis 3:1–15."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "The primordial chaos monster or cosmic force of disorder subdued by God. This is especially important for Old Testament dragon, sea-monster, Leviathan, and Rahab imagery and often functions as a background to Revelation.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 74:13–14",
        "Isaiah 27:1",
        "Isaiah 51:9–10",
        "Job 7:12; 26:12–13",
        "Genesis 1:21, where the related Hebrew term can mean great sea creatures rather than an evil being"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Oppressive political or imperial power, especially pagan Rome in interpretations of Revelation. The dragon may symbolize the satanic power operating through empire rather than Satan considered apart from his earthly agents.",
      "basis": [
        "Revelation 12:3, where the dragon’s seven heads and ten horns use political-beast imagery",
        "Revelation 13:1–4, where the dragon gives authority to the beast",
        "Daniel 7:1–8, 17–27 as the principal background for beasts representing kingdoms"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A particular hostile ruler or kingdom portrayed as a monstrous dragon, notably Pharaoh/Egypt and, in some translations, Nebuchadnezzar/Babylon.",
      "basis": [
        "Ezekiel 29:3 identifies Pharaoh as a great dragon or monster in the Nile",
        "Ezekiel 32:2 compares Pharaoh to a dragon or sea monster",
        "Jeremiah 51:34 portrays Nebuchadnezzar as swallowing Judah like a dragon in traditional translations"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A literal extraordinary animal, sea creature, giant serpent, or—in some modern creationist readings—a dinosaur, rather than a symbolic spiritual or political figure.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 1:21",
        "Job 40–41, when Behemoth or Leviathan is associated with dragon traditions",
        "Translation traditions rendering Hebrew tannin or related creature terms as “dragon”"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is a settled dominant Christian identification of the dragon in Revelation with Satan because Revelation states it explicitly. The term is not uniform across the entire Bible, however: Hebrew words traditionally translated “dragon” can denote sea monsters, serpents, jackals, ordinary great creatures, chaos imagery, or metaphorical rulers depending on context and translation."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "Satan (the Devil), the ancient serpent and adversary of God who opposes Christ and persecutes the people of God",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Revelation 12:3-9 (great red dragon identified as 'that ancient serpent called the devil, or Satan')",
    "Revelation 20:2 (dragon seized and bound, 'that ancient serpent, who is the devil, or Satan')",
    "Revelation 12:13-17; 13:2,4 (dragon as the power behind the beasts and persecutor of the woman/church)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Primordial chaos / sea monster (Leviathan-type figure representing disorder opposed to God's creative order)",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 27:1; 51:9",
        "Psalm 74:13-14; 89:10",
        "Job 41 (Leviathan)",
        "Ezekiel 29:3; 32:2 (Pharaoh as dragon/sea monster)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Pagan political power / empire (especially Rome as the persecuting world system empowered by or identified with the dragon)",
      "basis": [
        "Historicist and some preterist readings of Revelation 12–13",
        "Danielic beast imagery applied to successive empires"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Generic personification of evil or the forces of opposition without strict identification as a personal Satan",
      "basis": [
        "Broader apocalyptic and mythological background studies"
      ],
      "prominence": "rare"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "Christian tradition and biblical scholarship overwhelmingly treat the dragon of Revelation as Satan on the basis of the book's own explicit identifications; OT 'dragon'/tannin and Leviathan language supplies the mythic background and is commonly read as typological of the same adversary or of chaotic evil, but does not displace the primary NT identification."
}

BOOK ENTRY
A devouring kingdom.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: Satan himself, per Revelation 12:9.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Pharaoh, Ezek 29:3; Babylon, Jer 51:34) · see The Sign of Jonah, ch. 4

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Ezekiel 29:3 — Speak, and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers, which hath said, My river is mine own, and I have made it for myself.
Jeremiah 51:34 — Nebuchadrezzar the king of Babylon hath devoured me, he hath crushed me, he hath made me an empty vessel, he hath swallowed me up like a dragon, he hath filled his belly with my delicates, he hath cast me out.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
